summary: Specifies the base architecture for systems that implement IPsec, the family of protocols that secure IP traffic. It explains the security services offered, how security associations and policies work, and how the pieces fit together. It was a proposed standard, replaced by RFC 4301.

eli5.summary: IPsec is like a guarded armored truck for your data. This document is the master plan showing how the truck, the guards and the rule book all fit together.

subtitle: The 1998 master plan for IPsec: security associations, policy databases and how packets are protected at the IP layer.

tldr.problem: IP carries data with no built-in protection, so hosts and gateways need a common, interoperable way to authenticate, encrypt and control traffic at the IP layer.
tldr.mechanism: IPsec uses two protocols, AH and ESP, applied under rules from a Security Policy Database. Each protected one-way flow is a Security Association, found by an SPI, a destination address and a protocol.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2401 was obsoleted by RFC 4301 and updated by RFC 3168, so it is no longer the current IPsec architecture. The ideas it introduced, such as the SPD, the SAD and selectors, carry on.

today: RFC 2401 was a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 4301, and it was also updated by RFC 3168. For the current IPsec architecture, read the newer RFC; this one is useful for the original design.

sections.title: What IPsec Is For
sections.content:
RFC 2401 describes the base architecture of IPsec. IPsec gives cryptographic security to IPv4 and IPv6. Its services are access control, connectionless integrity, data origin authentication, protection against replays, confidentiality (encryption) and limited traffic flow confidentiality. Because they work at the IP layer, any higher protocol such as TCP, UDP, ICMP or BGP can use them.

The pieces are two traffic protocols, the Authentication Header (AH) and the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP), plus security associations, key management (including IKE) and algorithms for authentication and encryption. The RFC is explicit that it is not an overall Internet security architecture, and that security also depends on implementation quality, the operating system and good system management.

IPsec can run in a host or in a security gateway, an intermediate system such as a router or firewall that implements IPsec. It can be built into the IP stack, placed underneath it as a bump-in-the-stack (BITS), or put in an outboard device as a bump-in-the-wire (BITW).
sections.eli5: IPsec puts a lock and a seal on the mail at the very start of the trip, so any kind of message can be protected. This document explains how all the locks, keys and rules work together.

sections.title: Security Associations and Modes
sections.content:
A Security Association (SA) is a simplex, one-way "connection" that gives security services to the traffic it carries. An SA uses AH or ESP, but not both. Protecting a two-way conversation takes two SAs, one in each direction. An SA is identified by three things: a Security Parameter Index (SPI), the IP destination address and the security protocol (AH or ESP).

Each protocol has two modes. In transport mode the security header sits after the IP header and protects the upper layer protocols. In tunnel mode the SA is applied to an IP tunnel: there is an outer IP header and an inner one, with the security header between them. If either end of an SA is a security gateway, the SA MUST be tunnel mode. Hosts MUST support both modes, while a gateway is required to support only tunnel mode.

AH gives connectionless integrity and data origin authentication, with optional anti-replay, and also covers selected parts of the IP header. ESP can give encryption, and optionally authentication; the receiver may enforce anti-replay on an ESP SA. Either confidentiality or authentication may be omitted, but not both. When one SA is not enough, SAs are combined into an SA bundle by transport adjacency or iterated tunneling.
sections.eli5: An SA is a one-way secret tunnel between two computers, so a chat needs one for each direction. Tunnel mode wraps the whole letter in a new envelope, while transport mode only seals the letter inside.

sections.title: The Policy and SA Databases
sections.content:
The RFC describes two nominal databases. The Security Policy Database (SPD) says what to do with each packet, inbound or outbound. There are three choices: discard it, let it bypass IPsec, or apply IPsec. For protected traffic the SPD entry names the protocols, modes and algorithms. Entries are ordered and searched in the same order every time, so the first matching entry wins. If no policy matches a packet, it MUST be discarded.

The policy is matched using selectors: destination and source IP address (single, range or wildcard), name, data sensitivity level, transport protocol, and source and destination ports. Some may be "OPAQUE" when encryption hides them. Selectors set how fine-grained an SA is, from one SA for all traffic between two hosts to one per application.

The Security Association Database (SAD) holds the parameters of each active SA. Inbound lookup uses the outer destination address, the IPsec protocol and the 32-bit SPI. Entries also hold a sequence number counter, an anti-replay window, the algorithms and keys, an SA lifetime (a time, a byte count, or both), the mode and the observed path MTU.
sections.eli5: The policy book is a list of rules that says which mail to lock, which to drop and which to wave through. The SA list is the set of keys already in use.

sections.title: Processing Packets
sections.content:
For outbound traffic, IPsec matches the packet against the SPD to find the first policy. It then looks for a matching SA bundle, and creates one if none exists. If no key management entity is found, the packet is dropped. The packet is then processed by that bundle. A configuration that uses both NULL encryption and NULL authentication MUST NOT be allowed.

For inbound traffic, fragments are reassembled first. The SA is found from the outer destination address, protocol and SPI, and a failed lookup means the packet is dropped. After the SA has been applied, the receiver finds the matching inbound policy and checks that the SAs used are the kind and order the policy requires. Selector checks use the inner header for tunneled packets.

In tunnel mode the outer header's addresses name the tunnel endpoints, the inner header is left unchanged except for decrementing TTL, and IP options and extension headers of the inner packet are not touched. Four basic SA combinations MUST be supported: host to host, gateway to gateway, both together, and a remote host reaching a gateway and then a host behind it.

The RFC also covers ICMP error handling, including how path MTU messages must account for the added IPsec headers. Unauthenticated ICMP can cause denial of service, so it MUST be possible to configure whether to accept router ICMP. Two further sections cover auditing and use in multi-level secure systems.
sections.eli5: When a packet leaves, a guard checks the rule book, finds the right key and locks it. When one arrives, the guard finds the key from the label, unlocks it and checks that it was locked the way the rules demand.

sections.title: Keys and SA Management
sections.content:
IPsec mandates support for both manual and automated SA and key management. Manual management means a person configures keys and SA data on each system. It works for small, static setups, such as a company VPN between a few sites, but does not scale.

Wide deployment needs an automated, scalable protocol. The anti-replay features need automated SA management, and creating a new key means creating a new SA with a new SPI. The default is IKE under the IPsec domain of interpretation, though other automated protocols MAY be used. When one string of key bits serves several keys, the encryption key(s) MUST come from the first (left-most, high-order) bits and the authentication key(s) from the remaining bits.

For multicast, someone has to pick the SPI for the whole group and distribute the group's IPsec information by means this RFC does not define. The RFC also says it does not address how a host automatically discovers or verifies its security gateway: that must be configured by an administrator.
sections.eli5: Locks need keys. You can hand the keys out by hand, which is fine for a few friends, or use a robot that swaps keys for you, which works for everyone.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 1825
sections.content:
RFC 2401 obsoletes RFC 1825 and says the fundamental notions are unchanged. It differs substantially in detail and organization, with far more detail on compliance. It introduces the SPD, the SAD and the notion of SA selectors, and it is aligned with new versions of AH and ESP. Required combinations of AH and ESP are newly added, as are details of path MTU management.

The Security Considerations section states only that security considerations permeate the whole specification. A performance section notes that IPsec costs memory, computation and bandwidth, and that hardware may be needed for security gateways.
sections.eli5: This is the grown-up second edition of an earlier plan. It has the same big idea, but many more details and clearer rules.
